KV cache warmup/cold start behavior and mitigation

reserved GPUs, burst policies, and queueing backpressure
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: okay everyone welcome, thanks for scheduling. we've got 60 minutes, this is the deep dive on elastic provisioning and how kv cache warmup is affecting your tail latency, correct?
[00:09] Alex Garcia: yeah thanks Maya. we really want to understand why our p99 spikes so much when we have sudden ad-hoc inference traffic.
[00:14] Priya Menon: and whether reserving some GPUs vs fully hosted burst makes sense for cost and SLA.
[00:20] Jordan Liu: cool, i'll start with a quick framing then we can jump into Nova's traffic. quick note: i'll call the kv cache "kvcache" in the call, sorry if that sounds odd.
[00:28] Jordan Liu: architecturally there are two levers: provisioning (how quickly we spin up or reuse workers) and queueing policies (how long requests wait). on redwood we support immediate scale vs buffered queue. immediate scale tries to allocate extra worker capacity on demand, buffered queue holds requests for up to X seconds so batching can improve throughput.
[00:45] Samir Rao: can you explain the tradeoff there? we saw throughput improve but p99 went up during one test.
[00:51] Jordan Liu: yeah, so if you buffer to form bigger batches you'll reduce cost per-token and average latency, but you add queuing delay which hurts p95/p99 if you have some requests that can't afford waiting. also kvcache misses on newly allocated workers are expensive — they reinitialize kv shards or have to repopulate kvcache from prefix caching. that causes long tail spikes.
[01:13] Lina Zhou: how long does a kvcache repop take typically?
[01:17] Jordan Liu: depends on model sequence length and topology. for a medium-size chat model with a large kv footprint, cold kvcache populate on a new worker can add 150-400ms per request initially; if we include model warmup and kernel peg it can be 500-800ms in worst case for those first few requests. numbers vary if you use quantized kernels too.
[01:36] Alex Garcia: our current infra shows 700ms p99 jumps when traffic ramps from 100 qps to 400 qps.
[01:42] Jordan Liu: that aligns — you likely hit a mix of kvcache misses and auto-scale spin-up lag. the queueing model matters: if you let requests sit in a buffered queue for 200ms to hit a better batch size, you might still have the kvcache miss after dispatch, so you haven't eliminated the cold-start penalty.
[02:00] Ethan Ross: thought experiment: with reserved GPUs you pre-warm kvcache because workers are persistent. that removes the cache-pop penalty but you pay baseline cost. burst policies can be layered on top — reserved pool handles baseline RPS and hosted burst covers spikes.
[02:14] Priya Menon: our current deck uses 2 reserved A40-equivalent GPUs and then we throw burst to hosted; cost is high but p99s look stable in lab. question: how does redwood’s burst queue size affect fairness — do we prioritize reservation traffic?
[02:28] Maya Patel: good question. redwood routing can tag workload tiers: reserved traffic gets priority to reserved pool; burst will route to hosted pool when reserved capacity is saturated. the burst queue has configurable SLAs: you can set max wait, requeue policy, and fallback to a smaller model.
[02:42] Samir Rao: fallback to smaller model concerns us because accuracy matters. can we do quantized variants with similar quality?
[02:48] Jordan Liu: yes, we often recommend quantized 4-bit or 8-bit variants that we have validation profiles for. quality drop is workload dependent; our optimize tool can run a quick A/B with your eval set to estimate impact. quantization also reduces memory so more cache-friendly. but note: quantized kernels sometimes have slightly higher per-token latency due to dequantization overhead, so p99 may shift.
[03:09] Alex Garcia: hmm, okay. show us a concrete queueing model — you mentioned buffered queue with timeout.
[03:14] Jordan Liu: right — common model is multi-tier queueing: immediate route to reserved pool if capacity available; if not, place in burst buffer for up to T_burst milliseconds (we typically start with 200–400ms). If still not served, either scale up hosted workers (pay) or reject/fail depending on SLA. another variant uses soft time windows: low-latency requests get priority and avoid buffering.
[03:36] Priya Menon: our traffic has mixed intents: short single-turn queries (<=128 tokens) and long chat sessions (500+ tokens). what do you recommend for batching?
[03:45] Jordan Liu: for mixed workloads we use dynamic batching based on token budget, not just request count. short queries are grouped aggressively; long sessions often dispatched to dedicated lanes (or longer timeout windows) to avoid head-of-line blocking. We also recommend prefix cache warmers for common prompts to reduce cold miss rate.
[04:02] Alex Garcia: prefix warmers — we have a set of common prompts we can provide, but how do warmers work across different workers?
[04:07] Jordan Liu: warmers seed the kvcache on the pool by pre-running representative prefixes to populate KV entries. on reserved pools it's straightforward; on ephemeral hosted workers we have a background warm-up queue that warms new allocations before traffic is sent there when possible. we can't always guarantee warmers run before the first request in very sudden spikes.
[04:27] Samir Rao: question about backpressure — if our burst queue grows 3-5 seconds we start losing user experience. what are engineered guardrails?
[04:34] Ethan Ross: we implement multi-level backpressure: first, adaptive batching reduction (reduce wait time to lower queue length), second, overflow to cheaper quantized model, third, degrade non-critical routes, and finally reject after threshold. metrics and alerts drive automated policies.
[04:49] Priya Menon: can we simulate our production pattern? our spikes are short but high amplitude — 30s bursts that 4x load.
[04:56] Jordan Liu: absolutely. we'll need your RPS timeline, request-size distribution, and token-length percentiles. Jordan to run simulation using a queueing model (M/M/c with finite queue) and Redwood's runtime sim that includes kvcache cold-hit penalty.
[05:12] Alex Garcia: what's the expected latency improvement if we go from 2 reserved GPUs to 4? we don't want to overcommit.
[05:18] Maya Patel: depends on concurrency and model memory. if your baseline load consumes ~60% of two GPUs, one extra GPU may reduce queuing and eliminate most cold spin events; doubling to 4 would give more headroom and reduce host-level preemption but increases costs linearly. Our sim will quantify p95/p99 reduction for each tier.
[05:34] Lina Zhou: and how long does spin-up take on hosted? we measured 10-25s in an early test.
[05:39] Jordan Liu: hosted spin-up time varies by region and SKU; typical cold allocation is 7–18s for our fast pool, slower for larger GPUs. but note spin-up is not the only contributor — docker/container init, model load and kvcache populate add extra latency. in practice the first few requests to a fresh worker are expensive.
[05:57] Samir Rao: that 7–18s is worrying — our user SLAs can't tolerate that.
[06:01] Jordan Liu: that's why reserved pool or warm standby is common. another pattern: keep a minimal hot standby in hosted pool — a small number of warmed containers to absorb small spikes, which is cheaper than fully reserved GPUs.
[06:13] Priya Menon: hot standby seems attractive if cost-effective. will that still allow burst beyond standby?
[06:18] Maya Patel: yes, hot standby handles small spikes instantly; if spikes exceed standby, the rest goes through burst queue and then scale-up to hosted instances if configured. it's layered.
[06:28] Jordan Liu: for Nova's 30s high-amplitude bursts, a hot standby sized for typical peak amplitude can eliminate most p99 spikes. we can simulate cost tradeoffs: cost of 2 extra standby containers vs paying for hosted burst over time.
[06:41] Alex Garcia: let's talk quantization again — you mentioned memory helps kvcache. are we able to run mixed precision where larger instances hold full precision and small ones use quantized?
[06:49] Jordan Liu: yes, routing polices can direct high-fidelity requests to full-precision reserved workers, while best-effort or low-cost routes land on quantized workers. that preserves quality for critical flows.
[07:00] Lina Zhou: what's the operational burden of that routing? we have limited SRE resources.
[07:04] Ethan Ross: Redwood console exposes per-route routing rules and automatic fallbacks. operationally you set policy, we handle routing and metrics. you'll want an initial set of rules and a small SRE-owned playbook for incident handling.
[07:16] Samir Rao: on VPC/on-prem — we have a compliance constraint that certain user data can't leave our VPC. can we run private?
[07:24] Maya Patel: yes, Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem deployments. note: on-prem deployments often have longer startup times for new workers because of image pulls and local infra; so reserving capacity or keeping hot workers is even more important on-prem. network egress and KMS integration also add latency if not colocated.
[07:41] Priya Menon: if we move model hosting on-prem, do we lose the hosted burst option?
[07:46] Jordan Liu: you can combine Private with Hosted via a smart routing policy, but the burst to hosted depends on regulatory constraints. if data cannot leave VPC, burst to hosted is not allowed. some customers use encryption/proxying to allow bursts for non-PHI data only.
[08:01] Alex Garcia: our timeline is Q4 pilot. what would you recommend for an initial config?
[08:06] Jordan Liu: pilot recommendation: 2 reserved GPUs (baseline), 2 hot-standby containers in hosted pool, burst buffer T_burst=250ms, route critical traffic to reserved full-precision lane, non-critical to quantized lane. run simulations with your real traffic to validate.
[08:23] Priya Menon: sounds good. what about automatic warmers — can they be prioritized? we want warmers to run before user traffic to newly allocated workers.
[08:31] Jordan Liu: yes, we can set warmers as high-priority background jobs; on allocation they run first if the system detects pre-warm tokens available. It's best-effort in sudden 4x spikes though.
[08:41] Maya Patel: i'll add that to the doc and include the warm-up SLA expectations.
[08:46] Alex Garcia: any notes on kernel selection and quantized perf? we saw degraded throughput on one test.
[08:52] Jordan Liu: kernel selection depends on sequence length distribution and batch shapes. quantized kernels are often faster for dense compute, but if tokenization pattern leads to many short sequences with high overhead, the dequantize step can dominate. our profiler can run a few synthetic shapes to pick the best kernel.
[09:08] Samir Rao: profiling — what artifacts do you need from us?
[09:11] Jordan Liu: request histogram with timestamps, token length percentiles, current p95/p99 by route, and a small eval set of representative prompts. Priya, you said you'd provide those?
[09:21] Priya Menon: yes i'll gather and share by Friday.
[09:24] Jordan Liu: perfect. i'll run a sim that models M/M/c queue with finite buffer and per-allocation kvcache cold penalty. we'll produce p50/p95/p99 curves and cost estimate for reserved vs hot-standby.
[09:36] Lina Zhou: what about throttling — can we throttle non-critical flows at ingress to protect critical traffic?
[09:41] Ethan Ross: yes, you can set per-route rate limits and token quotas. we also support priority queues so critical flows jump ahead in buffer.
[09:50] Alex Garcia: ok last question — what failure modes should we watch for in pilot?
[09:55] Jordan Liu: common ones: under-provisioned kvcache capacity leading to repeated misses, hot-standby churn if warmers misconfigured, mis-sized burst buffer that either rejects too many requests or hides latency issues, and quantization causing subtle quality regressions for specific prompts. we'll surface these in the sim and the pilot checklist.
[10:15] Maya Patel: quick recap and next steps?
[10:18] Alex Garcia: recap from our side: provide traffic histograms and eval prompts; we'll review reserved GPU budgeting.
[10:24] Maya Patel: and from redwood: Jordan runs latency/cost sim, Maya shares pricing and reserved SKU options, Ethan will help configure warmers and queue policies in the trial.
[10:34] Jordan Liu: i'll also include a simulated hot-standby cost vs reserved cost table.
[10:38] Priya Menon: thanks, please include expected p99 improvements per configuration.
[10:42] Jordan Liu: will do.
[10:44] Alex Garcia: thanks all.
[10:45] Maya Patel: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule a follow-up to review the sim results next week.
[10:51] [end of recording]
